soil-bio-308.title: Five groups of soil health practices
soil-bio-308.text: Looking after soil well is not one trick but five families of them. Practices aimed at {{ref:soil-env-174}} should grow healthy plants, suppress pests or increase beneficial organisms, while reducing harm to the environment. They group into minimizing disturbance, keeping soil covered, maximizing biodiversity, managing water, and maintaining pH and nutrients without excessive loss. Organic matter practices come first for long-term sustainability, because each one has multiple benefits. Good physical condition and nutrient supply still need additional practices.

soil-bio-309.title: Why some crop residues last and others vanish
soil-bio-309.text: Only about 10-20% of a residue is converted to stable humus after decomposition. How fast it goes, and what it leaves, depends on its chemistry. Residues low in hemicellulose, polyphenols and {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, such as green {{ref:soil-agri-181}} and soybean residue, decompose fast. Their effect on organic matter is shorter than that of cornstalks or wheat straw. Manure with much bedding decomposes slowly and lasts longer in soil, and ruminant manure lasts longer than that of grain-fed chickens and hogs. Easily decomposed residues, manures, cover crops and straw boost aggregation more than compost, which has already decomposed, though compost raises water-holding capacity. A variety of residues is needed to feed diverse organisms, supply nutrients and promote aggregation. Lignin-rich straw or sawdust builds organic matter but needs added nitrogen. Otherwise the microbes run short and less becomes humus. See {{ref:soil-found-045}}.

soil-bio-320.title: When carbonates fool a carbon test
soil-bio-320.text: A soil test can report more organic carbon than the soil really holds. Carbonates decompose to CO2 during combustion-based analysis, and the instrument counts that CO2 as organic carbon. The problem arises on limestone-derived soils, including surface soils where {{ref:soil-water-038}} has exposed carbonate-rich horizons. Three approaches separate carbonate carbon from organic carbon: heat treatment, acid treatment and wet oxidation.

soil-bio-321.title: Epiphytes: plants that live on plants
soil-bio-321.text: Orchids never touch the ground, yet they live well. An epiphyte is a plant or plant-like organism that grows on the surface of another plant, taking moisture and nutrients from air, rain or accumulated debris. It uses the host, called the phorophyte, only for support and, unlike parasitic plants, draws no nourishment from it. It is not rooted in soil. Without soil it depends on fog, dew, rain, mist, nutrients leached or decomposed from rooted plants, and {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Holo-epiphytes never touch the ground, like orchids; hemi-epiphytes such as strangler figs spend only part of life off the ground. Epiphytes hold water in the canopy, reducing water input to the soil, and cool and moisten the host canopy, which may cut its transpiration.

soil-bio-322.title: Klebsiella oxytoca, a nitrogen fixer on barley roots
soil-bio-322.text: Klebsiella oxytoca is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium, closely related to K. pneumoniae and distinguished from it by indole production. It is a {{ref:soil-fert-102}}: it colonises plant hosts and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use. It has been shown to associate with the barley {{ref:soil-bio-143}} through an entire vegetative period. The bacteria adhere strongly to root hairs and less strongly to the elongation zone and the mucilage covering the root tip.

soil-bio-323.title: Isotope dilution: measuring by adding a known spike
soil-bio-323.text: Isotope dilution measures how much of a substance a sample holds by adding a known amount of an isotopically enriched form of it. The enriched standard dilutes the sample's isotopic composition. The method works from signal ratios, not intensities, and is an internal standardisation method, which gives it very high metrological standing. It is almost always paired with mass spectrometry. National metrology institutes use it to certify reference materials, and it helps when analyte recovery is low. The gains are measurable. In {{ref:soil-meth-029}} it can cut uncertainty from 5% to 1%, and isotope dilution mass spectrometry measures ratios to better than 0.25%. Double (reverse) dilution first calibrates the enriched spike against a natural-composition standard, because spikes come in small amounts of questionable purity. The principle is analogous to mark-and-recapture population estimates in ecology.

soil-chem-005.title: How fertilizers make soil more acidic
soil-chem-005.text: Feeding a crop can sour the soil beneath it. Fertilizer-induced acidification is the lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers. It is one cause behind {{ref:soil-chem-001}}. Most nitrogen fertilizers acidify, ammonium-based ones most of all: ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate, and {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. Urea and compost acidify less. {{ref:soil-fert-112}} of ammonium releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, which keep acidifying the soil. Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify and can slightly raise pH. Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH. Most commercial nitrogen fertilizers are acid forming, but many manures are not. Generally 4-7 pounds of lime neutralize the acid from each pound of nitrogen applied. Monoculture with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation. Sugarcane monoculture raised acidity, lowered fertility and shifted soil microbes.

soil-chem-120.title: Redoximorphic features: colors that record wet and dry
soil-chem-120.text: Soil keeps a diary of its wetness in color. Redoximorphic features are color patterns from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix color. They form by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix color is set by ferrous iron. A pattern counts as redoximorphic only once the processes that formed it are known or inferred. Reducing conditions give disrupted color with complex mottled patterns and points of color concentration, whereas aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes. As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles. Fluctuating water levels give red and yellow blotches mixed with gray. Continuous strong reduction from long-term waterlogging gives gleyed conditions in dark gray to blue to black. Eh, the voltage measured in a soil, expresses the potential for these reactions. Classification uses the features: Vertisols with {{ref:soil-class-155}} and redoximorphic features are Aquerts, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them. They provide critical information for soil interpretation. See also {{ref:soil-chem-118}}, {{ref:soil-found-025}} and {{ref:soil-found-028}}.

soil-chem-220.title: Managing salty soil where the groundwater is deep
soil-chem-220.text: Without a shallow salty water table, salinity is a problem of drying and leaching. Keeping soil continually moist, as with low-salt {{ref:soil-agri-015}} plus mulch, stops salt concentrating as the soil dries. Tolerant plants include barley, bermuda grass, oak, rosemary and willow, but only washing salt below the root zone removes it. Poorly draining subsoil may need drainage tiles, which discharge salty water that can harm downstream water. Seawater flooding after storm surges can make soils sodic, treated by gypsum, or lime where the soil is naturally acidic. See {{ref:soil-chem-008}} and {{ref:soil-chem-013}}.

soil-chem-222.title: Saline, sodic and saline-sodic: three ways soil goes salty
soil-chem-222.text: Two soils can look equally ruined and need opposite cures. Salt-affected soils are classed as saline, sodic or saline-sodic by total salt (EC) and sodium content (SAR, ESP). Saline soils have EC above 4 dS/m but SAR below 13 and ESP below 15%, with pH usually under 8.5 and flocculated colloids. Sodic soils have EC below 4 dS/m but SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%, and pH usually above 8.5 from hydrolysis of Na2CO3. Saline-sodic soils have EC above 4 dS/m, SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%. Their pH is usually below 8.5 and they stay flocculated. Sodium explains the difference. Hydrated Na+ between clay particles cancels the binding electrostatic forces, and extra water layers push the particles apart. That disperses sodic soil, and high pH also disperses organic matter. Saline soils stay aggregated with high infiltration, so they leach easily. Dispersed sodic and saline-sodic soils infiltrate poorly and usually need gypsum. Calcium replacing monovalent Na+ promotes aggregation and infiltration, and the displaced sodium and salts are leached. Saline drainage may be diverted through subsurface drains. Salt-tolerant crops such as barley or sunflower, and trees, can take up salts, but prevention is better than reclamation. Natural sources include mineral weathering, atmospheric deposition, seawater intrusion, saline groundwater and natural brines. Human sources include salty irrigation water, salty fertilizers, manure, {{ref:soil-fert-045}}, compost and road salt.

soil-chem-223.title: Aluminosilicates, the aluminium-silicon backbone of clays
soil-chem-223.text: Aluminosilicates contain anionic Si-O-Al linkages, with cations such as sodium, potassium or hydrogen balancing the charge. They occur as minerals, coal combustion products and synthetic materials, often zeolites, and matter technically as structural materials, catalysts and reagents. {{ref:soil-found-031}} like feldspar are the commonest example: a tectosilicate with potassium, sodium and calcium cations in a negatively charged network of silicon, aluminium and oxygen. Soil alumino-silica clays are aluminosilicates with a regular crystalline or quasi-crystalline structure, including {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, illite, vermiculite, chlorite and kaolinite. Naturally occurring microporous, hydrous aluminosilicate minerals are {{ref:soil-chem-199}}, whose varying Si/Al ratio tunes their properties. Each is a {{ref:soil-found-029}}.

soil-chem-238.title: How clay minerals differ in charge and surface area
soil-chem-238.text: Clay minerals of one family can differ enormously in how much they hold. Phyllosilicates differ mainly in cation exchange capacity, CEC, and in reactive surface area, which depend on {{ref:soil-chem-085}} and on whether the interlayer admits cations. Kaolinite has little substitution and does not expand, so its CEC is 2-16 cmol(+) per kg and its surface is only external, 5-15 m2 per g. Illite and chlorite have substantial substitution, but a tightly bound K+ or hydroxide interlayer blocks expansion, so CEC is limited: 20-40 for illite and 10-40 for chlorite. Smectite admits interlayer cations, giving CEC 60-120 and an internal surface of 570-660 m2 per g, and soils rich in it swell and shrink strongly. {{ref:soil-chem-095}} has CEC of 100-150 but expands little, because its charge, concentrated near the interlayer, binds cations tightly and restricts water entry. Fe/Al oxyhydroxides have CEC near 0-3 but 200-500 m2 per g of surface, and amorphous aluminosilicates range from 5 to 350 CEC.

soil-chem-239.title: Why Canadian clays came from the ice
soil-chem-239.text: Most of the layered clay minerals in Canadian soils did not form where they now sit. The continental glaciers delivered them in the parent material. Kaolinite, {{ref:soil-chem-135}} and chlorite come straight from the Canadian Shield, while others in the Interior Plains derive from degraded Cretaceous sediments. Interior Plains clay is mostly smectite, that same mineral, chlorite and some kaolinite. The older Devonian and Silurian sediments of the St. Lawrence Lowlands give that mineral, chlorite, vermiculite and kaolinite. Little alteration shows across regions. The exceptions are Podzolic and some Brunisolic and Gleysolic soils, where inherited chlorite weathers to expandable {{ref:soil-found-033}}.

soil-chem-240.title: Calcite, dolomite and the carbonates in soil
soil-chem-240.text: Where pH falls below 6.0, calcite is not usually found. Soil carbonates are mostly calcite and dolomite inherited from sedimentary rock, with some secondary precipitates in subsurface horizons. Calcite is sparingly soluble, more so at low pH. It dissolves from the upper solum and is redeposited lower as secondary calcite nodules. Dolomite also dissolves from the upper profile, supplying calcium to that calcite while magnesium is mostly leached or taken up by roots. Aragonite is neither common nor stable. Trona, Na2CO3, is highly soluble and found mostly in Solonetzic soils at pH about 9.5. Carbonates keep {{ref:soil-chem-052}}, exchangeable Ca and Mg, and pH above 7 high, precipitate phosphate and metals, and stabilize clays and structure. Their entry is {{ref:soil-found-034}}.

soil-chem-241.title: Phosphate minerals and where soil phosphorus goes
soil-chem-241.text: Phosphate forms over 300 minerals. The commonest pure primary ones are the apatites, Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH), with fluor-, chlor- and hydroxyapatite as the end members. Rock phosphate is mined for fertilizer. Soils typically hold 400-800 mg of phosphorus per kg, against a crustal average of 1050 mg per kg. Phosphate in soil, whether from rock or fertilizer, precipitates with calcium, aluminium and iron. Wet, sub-oxic soils form iron phosphates such as vivianite and {{ref:soil-chem-234}}. Acidic soils form aluminium phosphate, as in variscite. Calcareous soils form calcium phosphates such as brushite, which commonly precipitates where fertilizer is banded at high concentration.

soil-class-005.title: Soil type, the word many systems avoid
soil-class-005.text: Few terms in soil science are so common, or so slippery. A soil type is a taxonomic unit: all the soils that share a defined set of properties. In hierarchical systems it usually sits at a higher or intermediate level, split into subtypes and combined into higher categories. The first U.S. classification, by Whitney in 1909, did the reverse: there the soil type was the lowest level and the mapping unit. Systems also disagree on what defines a type. German soil systematics uses mainly features made by soil formation. The WRB and {{ref:soil-class-006}} add traits inherited from the parent material, and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} ignores origin. Horizons make a convenient basis, but some young soils lack clear ones, so types may rest on whole-profile properties. The WRB, for instance, defines one group by sand content alone. Many systems also define types that reflect human activity. Because the word is so general, many systems avoid it. In early U.S. mapping, 'soil type' was the original name of the {{ref:soil-agri-220}}, which records surface texture, slope, stoniness, saltiness and erosion.

soil-class-006.title: USDA soil taxonomy: six levels from order to series
soil-class-006.text: The United States sorts its soils into 12 orders, 47 suborders, about 185 great groups, about 1,000 subgroups, about 4,500 families and more than 14,000 series. USDA soil taxonomy is the classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}. It sorts soils by their properties into six levels, from most general to most specific: order, suborder, great group, subgroup, family and series. The lab manual describes it as a quantitative hierarchy running from 12 broad orders to more than 23,000 series, and says it helps carry management research between similar soils worldwide. Sources differ on the series count: the more than 14,000 above is the United States figure. It uses properties that can be measured: depth, moisture, temperature, texture, structure, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, clay mineralogy, organic matter and salt content. It is a hierarchical hybrid of natural and objective criteria, designed to guide land use and soil management, and it supplies the core criteria for U.S. soil map units. Order names end in -sol, and the criteria for orders reflect major differences in how soils formed. It builds on {{ref:soil-class-001}}, {{ref:soil-class-005}}, {{ref:soil-found-001}} and {{ref:soil-form-017}}. Guy Donald Smith, director of USDA soil survey investigations, originally developed it as a substantial revision of the strictly natural 1938 system. Work began by 1945. A series of approximations followed, the 7th in 1960, and the taxonomy appeared in 1975 with 10 orders and in 1999, revised, with 12.

soil-class-021.title: The FAO map legend that became a world system
soil-class-021.text: The first truly international soil classification began life as the key to a map. The FAO soil classification, developed by the {{ref:soil-env-372}}, is a supra-national system that generalizes how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors. It started as the legend of the FAO–UNESCO map of the world's soils, published from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million. Rudi Dudal led the 1974 legend. It gathered ideas from national systems, among them the diagnostic horizons of the USDA's 1960 '7th approximation'. Its 106 soil units were mapped as associations named for the dominant unit, with soil phases, three texture classes and three slope classes. Simple and broad, it fitted most soils from field descriptions alone. It was meant for continental maps, not local ones. The 1988 Revised Legend had 153 soil units in 28 major soil groupings, and it still underlies the Harmonized World Soil Database. United Nations projects applied the system, and many countries adapted it. Many of its names are known widely, with similar meanings. In the 1974 legend, thin soils on calcareous rock were called {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock were called {{ref:soil-class-040}}. The WRB replaced it in 1998.

soil-class-106.title: Vertisols, the clay soils that plow themselves
soil-class-106.text: Some soils turn themselves over without a plow. A Vertisol is rich in expansive clays that crack deeply when dry and swell when wet. It is both a USDA order and a Reference Soil Group of the {{ref:soil-class-016}}. It needs more than 30% clay to 50 cm and usually has a mollic epipedon, the dark topsoil of a Mollisol. Vertisols form in clay-rich material, often from basic rocks such as basalt, in seasonally humid or erratic climates. Alternate shrinking and swelling mixes the soil, a process called argillipedoturbation. Some end up with a very deep A horizon and no B horizon, and the subsoil heaves up as {{ref:soil-phys-030}}. Colors range from gray or red to deep black. Australians speak of 'black earths', East Texans of 'black gumbo' and East Africans of 'black cotton' soils. Found between 50°N and 45°S, Vertisols dominate eastern Australia, India's Deccan Plateau, parts of Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya and the lower Paraná. They cover 2.4% of the world's ice-free land. The heavy, unstable soil makes it hard for trees to grow, so the natural cover is grassland, savanna or grassy woodland. Very hard when dry and sticky when wet, Vertisols are hard to farm without irrigation, and most are grazed by cattle or sheep. Their near-impermeability when saturated suits rice. Shrink–swell damages buildings and roads, but it lets the soil recover quickly from compaction. Australians, who call them Vertosols, prize them as among the few soils not acutely short of phosphorus.

soil-env-181.title: Everything soil does for people and ecosystems
soil-env-181.text: About 50% of people live in houses built from soil. That is one of many jobs a {{ref:soil-found-077}} does, and together they are called soil functions: the general capabilities that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses. For food and biomass, soil stores and supplies nutrients, holds water in its pores and moderates temperature. It is a habitat and gene reserve for many organisms, and it turns the remains of dead plants and animals into simpler mineral forms other life can use. Soil also governs whether rain runs off or recharges aquifers, purifies wastes from a {{ref:soil-env-195}} and stores atmospheric carbon in organic matter. It supplies raw materials, and it carries cultural meaning, giving a sense of place and preserving artifacts of the past. Productive soil is limited in area, so extracting it needs to be controlled.

soil-env-188.title: Cover crops, compost and the toolkit of soil repair
soil-env-188.text: A field planted with one crop year after year slowly runs down. Monoculture depletes soil carbon and nutrients, because each crop takes up or returns only its own set of nutrients. Regenerative soil practices, many drawn from conservation agriculture, work to reverse that. Cover cropping, crop rotation, reduced disturbance, mulch retention and integrated nutrient management store more carbon and cut fossil fuel use. Permaculture uses mixed, native and perennial crops and avoids tilling, so microbes and roots stay in longer contact. {{ref:soil-env-326}}, from Allan Savory's work, claims planned grazing can improve soil health and reverse desertification; researchers dispute the desertification claim. Amendments, chosen to suit the soil's current state, lock up toxins, balance pH, add nutrients and encourage soil life. Inorganic ones improve texture and structure and limit heavy-metal availability. Wood ash, ground limestone and red mud are alkaline amendments; gypsum and dredged materials are mineral ones. Organic amendments such as mulch, compost, biochar, manure and biosolids improve biological activity, water permeability and structure. Biosolids are nutrient-rich, so they should be used sparingly.

soil-env-198.title: Persistent organic pollutants: the chemicals that reach the poles
soil-env-198.text: Chemicals never used in Antarctica or the Arctic turn up there anyway. Persistent organic pollutants, or POPs, are toxic organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and light-driven breakdown and persist in the environment. Most are pesticides or insecticides. Others are solvents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals, and only a few arise naturally, as from volcanoes and forest fires. They are typically halogenated, and their carbon-chlorine bonds resist being split by water or light. They dissolve poorly in water but readily in oils and fats, and solid particles capture them easily. That fat solubility lets them build up in fatty tissue. They volatilize from soils, vegetation and water, travel long distances in air and settle again. Indoors, levels in air and dust often exceed those in outdoor air and soil. The 2001 Stockholm Convention named a 'dirty dozen', including aldrin, chlordane, dieldrin, {{ref:soil-env-005}}, PCBs and dioxins, and newer POPs such as PFOS have been added since. Efforts focus more on banning their production and use worldwide than on removing them from the environment.

soil-fert-034.title: Using finished compost on fields and in beds
soil-fert-034.text: A field needs only a thin dusting of compost, about 6 mm (0.24 in). Compost applied is finished compost used on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients (see {{ref:soil-fert-028}}). On open fields it is broadcast in that thin layer and worked in before planting. A layer of 25 mm (0.98 in) or more is used to rebuild poor soils or control erosion. Added to soil, {{ref:soil-agri-139}} or peat, it improves tilth and supplies humus and nutrients. Tilled in, it raises organic matter and overall fertility. Compost is rarely used alone. It is mixed with sand, grit, bark, vermiculite, perlite or clay granules, and blends of 20-30% compost are common for transplanting seedlings. Seeding directly into compost is not advised: it dries fast, immature compost may hold germination-inhibiting phytotoxins, and undecomposed lignin may tie up nitrogen. Ready compost is dark brown or black with an earthy smell, and it can increase plant immunity to diseases and pests. Finished compost supplies little readily available nitrogen, since composting converts much N to stable organic forms while P and K availability is unchanged. It still releases other nutrients slowly and raises organic matter. Annual high rates set by nitrogen need overload soil with phosphorus and potassium, and salts may build up under high tunnels and greenhouses. Soil tests should guide a switch to legume cover crops.

soil-fert-253.title: Management intensive grazing: many paddocks, short stays
soil-fert-253.text: Pastures grazed continuously produce poorly. Repeated grazing of early regrowth depletes root reserves and weakens plants. Management intensive grazing rotates animals through many paddocks and does not regraze one until its plants have regrown. Cycles run from about a week or 10 days up to 6-8 weeks depending on season and weather, and dairy cows may get a fresh paddock after every milking. Harvesting and fertilizing need little equipment or labour, and electric fencing makes new paddocks quick to set up. Intensively managed pasture often lowers production cost despite the animals' foraging energy. Well-managed pasture combines perennial forage, no tillage and regular manure. New York soil health scores for organic matter, {{ref:soil-env-286}}, respiration, water capacity and aggregate stability were far higher under pasture ({{ref:soil-found-045}}). Stocking can reach about 100,000 pounds of animals per acre for 8-12 hours, used to suppress or kill poor plant species and let hooves help reseed more productive ones. Where animals roam large rangeland by day and are stocked densely at night, the carbon, nutrients and seeds they gather are excreted into the small area, boosting fertility and {{ref:soil-water-110}}. Grazing crop residue after grain harvest cuts feed costs and improves nutrient and carbon cycling. Cattle grazing corn residue in winter on the Great Plains raised soil health and yields. Swath grazing leaves annual crops such as barley and triticale cut in swaths for beef cattle, which improves forage access under deep snow.

soil-fert-254.title: How regular manure builds up phosphorus and potassium
soil-fert-254.text: Manure is not unbalanced; the trouble lies in nitrogen losses. Its nutrient ratios are roughly equal to crop needs, about 2:1 nitrogen to phosphorus. Buildup arises when nitrogen losses ({{ref:soil-fert-252}}) force high rates, so phosphorus and potassium accumulate in soil. Conserving nitrogen through timing, injection or incorporation lowers the manure rate needed, cutting P and K accumulation and the fertilizer N needed where P limits manure rates. After many years the soil test P and K can reach excessive levels, and all solutions need lower fertilizer P and P-containing amendments. Erosion of P-rich topsoil carries sediment and phosphorus to streams and lakes. Remedies include exporting manure and using N fertilizer or legumes, spreading manure more evenly across fields, rotating to alfalfa, which draws phosphorus down, {{ref:soil-agri-059}} to trap sediment, or sending manure to a neighbor or composting facility.

soil-fert-263.title: Nitrogen and phosphorus: two nutrients, opposite habits
soil-fert-263.text: Nitrogen moves; phosphorus mostly stays put. That contrast shapes how each is supplied, lost and managed. Nitrogen comes mainly from decomposing organic matter and can be added biologically by legumes ({{ref:soil-fert-099}}, {{ref:soil-fert-127}}). No biological process adds phosphorus, which also comes from soil minerals. Nitrate, the main form plants absorb, is very mobile. Phosphorus movement is very limited, and its available form is a small dissolved amount, mainly H2PO4- and HPO4 2-. Most N loss is nitrate leaching, denitrification or ammonia volatilization. Leaching dominates in sandy soils and denitrification in heavy loams and clays. Phosphorus is lost mainly in runoff and eroded sediment, but low losses have a high effect per unit on water quality because P often limits freshwater algae. P leaching matters in artificially drained fields: after years of excess manure or compost, P-saturated sandy soils leak P, and {{ref:soil-fert-211}} can flow through wormholes and cracks to drain lines. Cover crops store nitrogen that would otherwise leach, and mobilize P through mycorrhizae and store it for the next crop. Excess N pollutes water with nitrate, raises nitrous oxide from denitrification, wastes energy in manufacture, speeds loss of soil organic matter and is linked to more insect damage. Making, hauling and applying N fertilizer ({{ref:soil-fert-007}}) is about 30 percent of the energy used to grow corn.

soil-fert-270.title: Managing nitrogen and phosphorus: count, test, time, place, cover
soil-fert-270.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus behave differently in soil ({{ref:soil-fert-263}}), yet they need similar management. Take all nutrient sources into account, using soil, manure and compost tests, crop residue N, and the 4R principles of right rate, time, place and source, plus conservation practices. Place fertilizer below the surface, split N applications where leaching or denitrification threaten, and apply when leaching and runoff threats are minimal. Cover crops with minimal or no tillage improve structure, cut leaching, runoff and denitrification, and store N and P in organic form between cash crops. Reduced tillage also keeps mycorrhizal networks intact for P. Sod-type forage crops in rotation reduce nitrate leaching and P runoff, and {{ref:soil-agri-182}} such as cereal rye capture leftover nitrate. Time N close to crop uptake. Holding most fertilizer until a PSNT, sensor or model shows need lets sidedress N be applied only if wanted.

soil-fert-276.title: Nutrient flows: sources, destinations and the farm gate
soil-fert-276.text: Every bag of fertilizer and every truck of grain is a nutrient flow. A flow is the movement of carbon or nutrients from one place to another, linking a source with a destination. Flows happen on a farm, in a grassland or forest, or globally, within the idea of the {{ref:soil-fert-146}}. Buying fertilizer or feed brings nutrients onto the farm, and selling crops, meat or milk sends nutrients and carbon off it. Flows across the farm gate are managed on purpose. Others are unplanned, such as {{ref:soil-agri-022}} to groundwater or runoff carrying nutrients with eroded topsoil. Harvested crops fed to animals and manure returned to the land together make a cycle, because nutrients and carbon come back to the fields they left. Cycling is nearly 100% efficient in forests and natural grassland, but modern specialized farming has little real cycling, with large exports, long bare periods and bigger leaching and runoff losses. Organic matter is over half carbon, so soil nutrient cycling is tied to the {{ref:soil-env-102}}.

soil-fert-286.title: Where nutrient deficiencies tend to appear
soil-fert-286.text: Of the 17 elements all plants need, only nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are commonly deficient in soils. Sulfur deficiency is less common but not rare. Magnesium, zinc, boron and manganese can be lacking in certain regions. Geography helps predict which (see {{ref:soil-fert-169}}). Sulfur, magnesium and some micronutrient deficiencies are more common in highly weathered mineral regions, such as the southeastern United States and the tropics, or in high-rainfall regions. Sulfur deficiency is common on sandy coastal-plain soils and in low organic matter soils, as sulfur pollution from coal plants has declined. Calcareous higher-pH soils, especially in dry regions, need watching for iron, zinc, copper and manganese deficiency and for low phosphorus availability. {{ref:soil-fert-233}} is less common in young, little-weathered glaciated soils with moderate to low rainfall, as in the Dakotas.

soil-fert-289.title: Mineral nutrients: the elements beyond carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
soil-fert-289.text: In nutrition, a mineral is any chemical element other than carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen that an organism needs. A mineral counts only if it is bioavailable, meaning it can be absorbed, so it must be soluble or readily extractable. Metallic molybdenum has no nutritional benefit, while molybdates are sources. Plants and animals need similar minerals and enzymes, with differences. Legumes host molybdenum-containing {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, and animals use iron hemoglobin for oxygen but plants do not. Boron is essential to plants but not humans. Silicon is beneficial to most plants but usually not essential. Proving that an element is essential takes a biomolecule containing it with a testable function, because chemically similar elements can be taken up without being essential. Fertilizers are often tailored to the mineral deficiencies of particular soils, such as molybdenum, manganese and zinc.

soil-fert-291.title: Closing the loop on the farm
soil-fert-291.text: Better on-farm nutrient cycling aims to cut long-distance {{ref:soil-fert-276}} and return nutrients as residue or manure to the fields they came from. It extends {{ref:soil-fert-192}}. Losses fall when infiltration and root health rise through organic matter and soil physical management. Apply only the irrigation water needed to refill the root zone, since excess causes runoff and leaching. Rotations with cover crops, perennial grasses and legumes leach less nitrogen than annual row crops such as corn and soybeans. Test manures and credit their nutrients, test soils regularly, and apply most nitrogen near crop uptake. Add animals to crop farms and match their numbers to the land base. Feeding crops to animals exports far fewer nutrients than selling crops, but animals fed on purchased feed overload a farm. Local organic materials, composting to cut manure weight and volume for transport, compost exchanges and neighboring farm partnerships also help balance flows.

soil-fert-292.title: Fertilizer or organic source: choosing what to apply
soil-fert-292.text: Commercial fertilizers such as urea, triple {{ref:soil-fert-094}} and muriate of potash are convenient, easy to blend, predictable and precise in timing and rate. They have drawbacks. Common nitrogen materials are acid forming, nitrogen fertilizer takes 25%-50% of the energy in growing corn, and high solubility can cause salt or ammonia damage to seedlings and greater losses if mismanaged. Slow-release forms, such as sulfur- or polymer-coated urea, and {{ref:soil-fert-013}}, better match supply to crop needs. Organic sources are the nutrients in crop residues, manures and composts. Organic farmers replace synthetic fertilizers with minerals like greensand, granite dust and rock phosphate, or with bone, fish, soybean and blood meal. The cheapest source is not always best: anhydrous ammonia is hard to inject in stony soil, {{ref:soil-fert-206}} gives 18% N with phosphorus, and potassium magnesium sulfate suits fields needing magnesium but no lime.

soil-form-034.title: Cryoturbation: how frost churns the ground
soil-form-034.text: In the frozen north, the soil mixes itself. Cryoturbation is frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in soils with permanently frozen ground. It occurs to some degree in most Gelisols, whose name comes from Latin gelare, to freeze. Autumn freezing forms ice wedges in the most erodible parts of the parent rock. In summer the {{ref:soil-env-146}} lets loosened material move both down and up. Moisture moves from the warm surface to the cold top of the frozen layer, drying the upper soil into a granular structure with ice lenses. These lenses grow by drawing unfrozen water along a thermal gradient, displacing and mixing mineral and organic material at the ice-water interface. Separation of coarse from fine material produces {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. Cryoturbation is the dominant force in that layer and tends to make it uniform in composition. It is strongest on exposed sites and weak in sheltered valleys: Turbels show it in over one-third of that layer, with distorted {{ref:soil-form-005}}, Orthels in less. In frost boils it can bring base-rich water to the surface, neutralizing acidity and replenishing nutrients. In effect, ice scrambles the layers described in {{ref:soil-found-001}}.

soil-form-066.title: Laterization: rain, drought and millions of years
soil-form-066.text: Laterization was most active from the mid-Tertiary to the mid-Quaternary, 35 to 1.5 million years ago, and it has not stopped. It is the prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite. It needs high temperatures and heavy rainfall alternating with dry seasons. Rain leaches the rock, and in the dry season {{ref:soil-phys-252}} lifts the dissolved ions to the surface. Acid dissolves the host minerals. Hydrolysis precipitates insoluble iron and aluminum oxides, while sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium are leached away. Solutions of the right pH dissolve silica in preference to the iron and aluminum oxides, leaving mainly those two metals behind. The first products are weathered rocks called saprolites, and quartz is the most abundant mineral surviving from the parent rock. Gentle crests and plateaus help by protecting the weathered cover from erosion. The parent rock shapes the result. Mafic, iron-rich rocks yield {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, granitic iron-poor rocks yield aluminum ores, and ultramafic rocks yield nickel laterites. The process slowed with abrupt global cooling and continues today at a reduced rate.

soil-form-141.title: Feldspar: the rock mineral that becomes clay
soil-form-141.text: Feldspars make up about 60% of the Earth's crust and 41% of the continental crust by weight. They are rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium. The commonest are the sodium-calcium plagioclase feldspars and the potassium-sodium alkali feldspars. Formed at high temperature, they are unstable at the surface, especially plagioclase, so they weather easily. Hydrolysis, described in {{ref:soil-form-172}}, turns them into clay minerals including {{ref:soil-chem-094}}, {{ref:soil-chem-091}} and {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, and because feldspars are so abundant, clays are abundant too. Clay-replaced feldspar looks chalky beside glassy unweathered grains. Feldspar-rich sediment therefore points to little chemical weathering before burial.

soil-form-156.title: From summit to toeslope: positions on a hillside
soil-form-156.text: A hillside is not one soil but a sequence. The summit is the level top of an upland feature, and the shoulder is the convex, erosional edge leading to the backslope. The backslope is the steepest part, shaped mainly by {{ref:soil-water-053}} and running water. Below it, the footslope is gently inclined and concave, where colluvium and alluvium accumulate, and the toeslope is a constructional surface where alluvium collects. Beyond lies a flood plain, built of sediment deposited during floods, and a stream terrace is a level strip of an abandoned one. This is {{ref:soil-form-045}} made concrete.

soil-form-157.title: Effective precipitation: why wetter and cooler leaches more
soil-form-157.text: Rainfall alone does not decide how leached a soil is. Precipitation and temperature together set how much water moves down through it. Leaching, described in {{ref:soil-form-050}}, moves soluble salts down the profile and can carry suspended clay into the subsoil, deeper with more precipitation. It lowers pH, removes basic cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) and lowers nutrient content, so desert soils are little leached and humid forest soils extensively. Higher temperature raises {{ref:soil-water-161}}, so with equal rainfall the cooler region has more effective precipitation and more leached soils. In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes get less direct sun and so tend to be more weathered, deeper and more leached than warmer, drier south-facing ones. All of this is {{ref:soil-form-044}} in action.

soil-form-158.title: How a soil changes as it grows old
soil-form-158.text: A soil has an age, and it shows. Parent material has no horizons. A young soil, about 10 to 1,000 years old, has a slight profile. A mature soil, 1,000 to 10,000 years, has a well-developed one, and an old soil, 10,000 to 100,000 years, an extensive one. Typical profiles run C R, then A C R, then O A Bt C R, then O A E Bs C R. The chemistry changes too. In a young soil humus accumulates and carbonates leach. In a mature soil humus peaks and clays leach, with maximum illuviation. In an old soil humus declines, carbonates are gone and the surface is very acidic. Crop productivity follows: low to moderate in young soil, maximal in mature soil and low in old soil. Once vegetation grew, nitrogen entered from rain and from lichens, algae and legumes, and organic matter built a dark A horizon as rain leached calcium and magnesium carbonates. Where soils stay highly calcareous, the lime limits clay leaching and slows development. On permeable material, clay moved from the A into the B and formed an {{ref:soil-class-045}}. This is {{ref:soil-form-047}} at work.

soil-form-160.title: How people change soil
soil-form-160.text: Plow up a forest or grassland and the soil usually loses organic matter; globally about 30% of the original {{ref:soil-env-108}} is lost. Human use transforms soils mainly through land conversion, erosion, mining and construction. Erosion removes the organically enriched surface layer, losing the most fertile soil and sometimes exposing a growth-limiting layer such as a high-sodium one. Where the eroded soil lands, it over-thickens lower slopes and buries the original topsoil under less fertile subsoil, giving a cumulic soil. Soils heavily disrupted by people, as by mining or pipelines, are termed anthropogenic, and reconstructed soils inevitably differ from the original profile. People thus join the {{ref:soil-form-043}}.

soil-form-162.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soil-form-162.text: No other part of Canada has soils as varied as British Columbia and Yukon, thanks to a varied geologic history, rugged terrain and a wide climate range. The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system. Podzols have the largest extent in British Columbia, on {{ref:soil-chem-004}} under cool, humid conditions, and Luvisols are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest. Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks, while Chernozems occur only in the arid Central Interior. Regosols mark landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta, and drained Gleysols in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils. Mining leaves Anthroposols; in metal mining the chief concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-134}} weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

soil-form-163.title: Soils of the Prairie Provinces
soil-form-163.text: In southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, over 80% of the land is agricultural, the most heavily converted in Canada, and the kind of farming follows soil capability. True prairie covers only the southern part. About one-third of the region sits on Canadian Shield rock and two-thirds on sedimentary rock; igneous rock yields acidic sandy, gravelly parent materials, sedimentary rock neutral to alkaline loamy ones. Chernozems dominate the southern grassland, Luvisols the northern mixed forest, Brunisols the acidic Shield and Organic Cryosols the cold, saturated peats near Hudson Bay. The pattern is set by bedrock and by the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera. Crops once centred on spring wheat with summerfallow; today canola, pulses and flax are grown, with continuous cultivation and {{ref:soil-agri-099}} or no-till. Under the Canada Land Inventory, classes 1 to 4 sustain field crops and classes 5 and 6 suit only forage.

soil-form-166.title: Soils of Ontario
soil-form-166.text: Ontario's soils are young, laid down by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet. The ice retreated northeast, exposing southern Ontario as much as 13,000 years ago and the far north about 8,500 to 6,500 years ago. Three ecozones now dominate. The Hudson Plains (about 25% of Ontario) are cold and semi-arid, with clayey and silty glacio-marine materials over neutral to alkaline limestones. The Boreal Shield (about 66%) lies on acidic, weathering-resistant Precambrian gneiss and granite, and Dystric Brunisols dominate the west. The Mixedwood Plains (about 9%) rest on carbonate-rich limestones, so parent material matters most; they hold the province's most productive farmland and its major cities. The Guelph series, a Brunisolic Gray-Brown {{ref:soil-class-133}} formed in loam to silt loam moraine, became Ontario's provincial soil in 2015.

soil-form-172.title: Hydrolysis: how water cracks minerals open
soil-form-172.text: Water does more than wet a mineral; it can break it. Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds. One fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide. It is the reverse of condensation, which joins molecules by removing water. The lab manual says all minerals weather this way, and that hydrolysis is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals. In one example, {{ref:soil-form-143}} and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-. This is a main route of {{ref:soil-found-058}}. Hydrolysis also drives {{ref:soil-chem-076}}. Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids: trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with a pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly. In acid sulfate soils, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as jarosite release H+ this way. In alkali soils the carbonate anion hydrolyses to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH. The enzyme {{ref:soil-fert-224}} catalyzes the hydrolysis of {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and highly alkaline soils, pH about 8.2 or higher, increase it.

soil-found-027.title: What a soil's color says about its history
soil-found-027.text: A soil keeps its history on its surface, and color is how it shows it. Dark brown or black usually means high organic matter, which coats mineral particles and darkens them; accumulated charcoal also turns soil black. An Illinois handheld chart links nearly black soil to 3.5-7% organic matter, dark brown to 2-3% and yellowish brown to 1.5-2.5%. Red points to iron accumulation or oxidation in well-aerated soil, and yellow also reflects iron, in less oxygen-rich settings. Gray or blue marks saturated, anaerobic soil where iron has been reduced or depleted. Green can come from iron reduction or from minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-196}}, melanterite and celadonite. White is common where salts or carbonates accumulate, often in arid places, and {{ref:soil-chem-197}} can color acidic soils yellow. A B horizon takes its color mainly from {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, usually brownish or reddish. Sodium helps humus disperse and reach more minerals, so it influences how deep the dark color extends.

soil-found-038.title: Scratch, streak and shine: telling minerals apart
soil-found-038.text: Color is the most obvious thing about a mineral, and often not diagnostic at all. Mineral identification tells minerals apart by physical properties: crystal habit, hardness, luster, color, streak, cleavage and specific gravity. Hardness is usually measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond. The streak is the color of the powdered mineral, and traces of other elements and weathering do not change it. Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or X-ray diffraction analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming. Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that X-ray diffraction can determine.

soil-found-042.title: Kaolinite, smectite, illite: the main kinds of clay
soil-found-042.text: There are about 30 types of pure clay, but nature rarely serves one alone. Most natural deposits mix several of them with other weathered minerals. The main kinds of clay are grouped by their dominant {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, each with its own entry later: {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, {{ref:soil-chem-093}} and {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. A few others, among them talc and pyrophyllite, are sometimes also classed among them. Chemical and physical tests struggle to tell them apart. {{ref:soil-chem-228}} identifies them most easily. One clay keeps a calendar. Varved clay shows visible annual layers laid down seasonally, and is common in former glacial lakes.

soil-found-047.title: Organic matter that minerals keep for centuries
soil-found-047.text: Some carbon in soil lasts a few years; some lasts centuries. The difference often lies in what it is stuck to. Mineral-associated organic matter is {{ref:soil-found-045}} chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces. It is thought to consist of small plant and microbial molecules. They bond to charged mineral surfaces or are locked inside aggregates, crumbs of soil particles stuck together. Binding to minerals makes this carbon harder for decomposers to reach. So it resists microbial breakdown and stays in the soil's store of carbon. It typically persists for centuries. By contrast, {{ref:soil-bio-118}}, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only a few years to decades.
